questions.stem: In Australia, monetary policy is set by:
options: the Senate, which votes on the government's spending bills
the Reserve Bank of Australia, which decides the cash rate target
the Australian Treasury, which drafts the annual federal Budget
the Australian Taxation Office, which collects income tax revenue
questions.explanation: Monetary policy means influencing the cost and availability of money, and in Australia the Reserve Bank Board sets a target for the cash rate to pursue low inflation and full employment. Naming the Treasury is the most tempting error, because Treasury is central to economic policy — but its Budget work is fiscal policy (taxing and spending), not interest rates. The cue: if the tool is the cash rate, the body is the RBA; if the tool is tax or government spending, it is the government.

questions.stem: Fiscal policy is best described as the government's use of:
options: the exchange rate to influence the price of exports and imports
taxation and government spending to influence economic activity
the cash rate target to influence borrowing and saving decisions
laws about competition and fair trading to influence business conduct
questions.explanation: Fiscal policy is the deliberate use of the Budget — the revenue side (mainly taxes) and the expenditure side (mainly government spending) — to influence the level of economic activity. Referring to the cash rate is the classic mix-up: that is monetary policy, run by the RBA, not a Budget measure. Remember that fiscal comes from the Latin for treasury, so fiscal policy lives in the Budget.

questions.stem: In the circular flow model of the economy, which group are all leakages (withdrawals) from the flow of income?
options: government spending, exports and investment
taxation, exports and government spending
savings, taxation and imports
investment, exports and savings
questions.explanation: Leakages are income that households receive but do not pass straight back to domestic firms: money saved, money paid in tax, and money spent on goods produced overseas. The list containing investment, exports and savings is tempting because savings is genuinely a leakage, but investment and exports are injections, which add spending back into the flow. A quick check: does the money leave the domestic spending stream (leakage) or enter it from outside (injection)?

questions.stem: The RBA raises the cash rate target in response to high inflation. The most likely intended effect is that:
options: borrowing costs rise, so households and firms reduce spending and price pressures ease
saving becomes less rewarding, so households spend more and businesses cut prices
the government collects more tax revenue, which it uses to lower retail prices
loans become cheaper, so business investment rises and supply quickly increases
questions.explanation: A higher cash rate feeds through to higher interest rates on loans and deposits, which discourages borrowing, raises mortgage repayments and encourages saving; the resulting fall in demand reduces upward pressure on prices. The option about saving becoming less rewarding reverses the relationship — higher rates make saving more attractive, not less. Cue: rates up means spending down, which is contractionary.

questions.stem: A federal Budget is in deficit when, over the financial year:
options: government revenue is greater than government spending
the value of imports is greater than the value of exports
household savings are greater than household borrowings
government spending is greater than government revenue
questions.explanation: A Budget deficit is a fiscal outcome: the government's outlays exceed the receipts it raises, mainly through taxation, so it must borrow to cover the gap. The option about imports exceeding exports describes a trade deficit, which is about Australia's transactions with the rest of the world, not the government's accounts. Check whose accounts the word 'deficit' refers to before answering.

questions.stem: In a five-sector circular flow model, total leakages (savings + taxation + imports) are greater than total injections (investment + government spending + exports). This suggests that:
options: inflation will accelerate as spending on domestic production increases
the level of economic activity will contract, with output and incomes falling
the level of economic activity will expand, with output and incomes rising
the economy is in equilibrium, with output and incomes remaining steady
questions.explanation: When more income leaks out of the flow than is injected back in, firms sell less, cut production and reduce the incomes they pay households, so activity contracts. Saying the economy is in equilibrium is tempting because equilibrium is the model's headline rule — but equilibrium requires leakages to equal injections, not merely to be compared. Bigger leakages means the flow shrinks; bigger injections means it grows.

questions.stem: One reason monetary policy is often described as more flexible than fiscal policy is that:
options: monetary policy affects the whole economy, while fiscal policy affects only one state
monetary policy takes effect instantly, while fiscal policy takes several years to work
the RBA Board can change the cash rate at its regular meetings, without new legislation
the RBA can change tax rates immediately, while spending changes need parliament
questions.explanation: Major fiscal changes usually require Budget decisions and legislation passed by parliament, whereas the RBA Board meets regularly and can adjust the cash rate on the day it decides to, making the tool quicker to redirect. The claim that monetary policy works instantly is wrong: changes in the cash rate typically take many months to flow through to spending and inflation. Flexibility here means how fast the decision can be made, not how fast the results appear.

questions.stem: During a downturn, the federal government increases spending on road construction and lowers income tax rates. Using the circular flow model, this policy is best described as:
options: expansionary fiscal policy that raises injections and reduces leakages, lifting national income
contractionary fiscal policy that raises leakages and reduces injections, lowering national income
expansionary monetary policy, because the cash rate falls whenever income tax rates are cut
neutral in the circular flow, because government spending is counted as a leakage, not an injection
questions.explanation: Government spending is an injection into the circular flow and taxation is a leakage, so spending more while taxing less increases injections and reduces leakages, boosting household income and total spending — the definition of expansionary fiscal policy. The option calling it contractionary reverses the effect: contractionary fiscal policy means cutting spending or raising taxes, which is what a government does to slow an overheating economy, not to fight a downturn. The option naming monetary policy confuses the two tools: monetary policy is the RBA's setting of the cash rate, and a tax cut does not change the cash rate. Cue: if the Budget (spending and taxes) is being changed, it is fiscal policy.

questions.stem: The Reserve Bank of Australia conducts monetary policy with a stated inflation target. That target is to keep consumer price inflation:
options: at exactly 0 per cent in every calendar year
between 2 and 3 per cent in every single quarter without exception
equal to the unemployment rate each financial year
between 2 and 3 per cent, on average, over time
questions.explanation: The RBA's medium-term goal is consumer price inflation of 2–3 per cent on average over time, which gives it room to look through short-term price shocks while keeping the value of money reasonably stable. The option demanding 2–3 per cent in every single quarter is tempting because it uses the right numbers, but the target is deliberately an average over time, not a quarter-by-quarter rule. Zero inflation is not the goal, because mild inflation helps wages and prices adjust. Cue: whenever you see the target, the words 'on average, over time' belong with it.

questions.stem: Which of the following Australian government or RBA actions is an example of monetary policy?
options: The RBA board changes the cash rate target at its meeting
The federal government raises the rate of the GST
The federal government increases the age pension payment
The federal government funds construction of a new hospital
questions.explanation: Monetary policy is the RBA's use of the cash rate target to influence interest rates, borrowing, spending and ultimately inflation and employment. Raising the GST is tempting because it changes how much money people have to spend, but taxation is a fiscal policy tool controlled by the government, not the RBA. Cue: ask who acts — if it is the Treasurer or Parliament changing taxes or spending, it is fiscal; if it is the RBA changing the cash rate, it is monetary.

questions.stem: A worker earning $50,000 pays an average of 15 per cent of income in income tax, while a worker earning $200,000 pays an average of 30 per cent. This shows the income tax system is:
options: indirect, because the tax is collected from wages by employers
progressive, because the average rate of tax rises as income rises
regressive, because the higher earner pays a larger total amount
proportional, because both workers pay tax on the same income base
questions.explanation: A progressive tax takes a higher proportion of income as income rises, which is exactly what the rise from 15 per cent to 30 per cent shows; the revenue helps fund services and transfers that support living standards. Calling it regressive is tempting because the higher earner pays more dollars, but regressive means the proportion falls as income rises. Cue: judge progressivity by the percentage of income paid, not the dollar amount.

questions.stem: Inflation has climbed to 6 per cent while unemployment is unusually low. The RBA responds by raising the cash rate. The main short-term cost of this response is likely to be:
options: an increase in the Budget deficit caused directly by the rate rise
a rise in inflation as borrowers pass on higher loan repayments permanently
slower economic growth and some rise in unemployment as spending is dampened
an immediate fall in the general price level back to previous levels
questions.explanation: Tighter monetary policy cools inflation by reducing borrowing and spending, and weaker demand means firms hire less, so slower growth and higher unemployment are the usual short-term trade-off. Expecting prices to fall back to previous levels confuses lower inflation with deflation: rate rises aim to slow the rate of price increases, not reverse past increases. Cue: inflation falling means prices are still rising, just more slowly.

questions.stem: One channel through which an RBA rate rise affects the economy is the exchange rate. All else equal, higher Australian interest rates tend to:
options: push the Australian dollar down, making imported goods more expensive for households
leave the exchange rate unchanged, since the dollar is fixed against the US dollar
raise the dollar and therefore make Australian exports more competitive overseas
attract foreign investors to Australian assets, lifting the dollar and making imports cheaper
questions.explanation: Higher Australian rates increase the return on Australian dollar assets, raising demand for the dollar, and a stronger dollar lowers the price of imports, which helps reduce inflation. The option saying the dollar falls reverses the flow of funds; higher returns attract capital rather than repel it. The option about exports is wrong because a stronger dollar makes Australian exports dearer, not more competitive. Cue: higher rates → capital inflow → dollar up → imports cheaper, exports dearer.

questions.stem: Which is the federal government using transfer payments to redistribute income?
options: Blocking a merger between two supermarket chains to protect competition
Allowing banks to raise mortgage rates in line with their funding costs
Paying the Age Pension to eligible retirees, funded from taxation
Lowering the cash rate so households pay less interest on home loans
questions.explanation: A transfer payment is money paid by government to households without any good or service being supplied in return, funded from tax revenue; the Age Pension is a clear example and it redistributes income towards people with low earning capacity. The cash rate option is tempting because it also affects household budgets, but the cash rate target is monetary policy set by the Reserve Bank, not a payment made by government to households. The cue is to ask who pays whom: a transfer payment involves government money going directly into a household's bank account.

questions.stem: During a recession, and without any new decisions being announced, the amount the Australian Government pays in unemployment benefits rises while the income tax it collects falls. This is best described as:
options: Automatic stabilisers cushioning the fall in household incomes and spending
Discretionary fiscal policy, because new Budget measures have been legislated
Monetary policy, because the Reserve Bank is supporting demand in the economy
Contractionary fiscal policy, because the Budget balance moves further into deficit
questions.explanation: Automatic stabilisers are features already built into the tax and welfare systems that respond to economic conditions on their own: incomes fall so tax paid falls, and more people qualify for benefits, which props up spending without any new law. The discretionary fiscal policy option is the most tempting because both involve the Budget, but discretionary policy requires a deliberate new decision such as a fresh spending program or tax cut. The cue is the phrase 'without any new decisions announced' — that signals automatic, not discretionary.

questions.stem: The economy is already operating close to full capacity, with unemployment unusually low. The government announces a large, debt-funded increase in spending on new projects. Which outcome is most likely in the short term?
options: Unemployment falls to zero because every extra worker is now needed
The Reserve Bank cuts the cash rate to reinforce the government's spending
Demand rises faster than supply can respond, adding to inflation pressure
Prices fall quickly because extra projects increase the supply of goods
questions.explanation: Expansionary fiscal policy adds to aggregate demand, but when the economy is already near capacity there are few spare workers and resources, so the extra demand tends to push prices up rather than output. The option about falling prices is tempting because infrastructure projects do add to productive capacity, but that effect takes years, not months. The cue is timing: capacity effects are long term, while spending injections hit demand almost immediately.

questions.stem: The unemployment rate is calculated as:
options: People on income support, as a share of workers
Working-age people not in the labour force, as a share of it
Unemployed people, as a share of the labour force
People without a paid job, as a share of the population
questions.explanation: The labour force is people who are employed plus those who are unemployed (without work, available and actively looking), and the unemployment rate is the unemployed share of that group. Using the total population is the common error: it wrongly counts children, retirees and full-time students who are not looking for work. Remember the denominator is the labour force, not everyone.

questions.stem: An economy has a working-age population of 20 million, a labour force of 13.5 million, and 621,000 people unemployed. The unemployment rate is closest to:
options: 6.2 per cent
4.6 per cent
3.1 per cent
67.5 per cent
questions.explanation: Divide the unemployed by the labour force: 621,000 ÷ 13,500,000 ≈ 0.046, or about 4.6 per cent. The 3.1 per cent answer comes from dividing by the working-age population instead of the labour force, which is the classic denominator error, while 67.5 per cent is the participation rate (13.5 ÷ 20). Always identify the labour force figure first, then divide.

questions.stem: Over a year, average wages in Australia rise by 3 per cent while the CPI rises by 5 per cent. What has happened to real wages?
options: Real wages are unchanged, because wage rises are automatically indexed to the CPI
Real wages have risen by 8 per cent, because wage growth and inflation are added together
Real wages have fallen, because prices rose faster than pay, so purchasing power is lower
Real wages have risen by 3 per cent, because pay packets are larger than they were
questions.explanation: Real wages compare nominal pay growth with inflation: with pay up 3 per cent and prices up 5 per cent, each dollar buys less, so real wages fall by roughly 2 per cent. The option saying real wages rose 3 per cent confuses nominal growth with real growth by ignoring prices altogether. The cue word is 'real' — it always means the figure has been adjusted for inflation.

questions.stem: A furniture retailer sees that consumer confidence has fallen sharply, unemployment is edging up and retail sales growth has stalled. Which business decision is the most consistent response to these indicators?
options: Delaying a planned new store and ordering smaller volumes of stock for the coming season
Immediately opening three new stores, because weak indicators guarantee cheaper customers
Sharply raising prices on all items, because household demand always strengthens in downturns
Signing long-term contracts for double the usual stock, because falling confidence lifts spending
questions.explanation: Indicators like consumer confidence, unemployment and retail sales are leading or coincident signals of household demand, so weak readings suggest firms should hold back on expansion and inventory to avoid unsold stock and unused capacity. The option about raising prices assumes demand rises in a downturn, which reverses the actual relationship — weaker confidence usually means consumers cut discretionary spending like furniture. Ask what the indicators say about future sales before deciding whether to expand or contract.

questions.stem: An employment report shows that the number of people employed rose by 30,000 over the month, yet the unemployment rate also rose. The best explanation is that:
options: The working-age population must have shrunk during the month, distorting the calculation
Inflation must have risen at the same time, since prices and unemployment always move together
The labour force grew by more than 30,000 as extra people began actively looking for work
The number of employed people must in fact have fallen, so the report contains an error
questions.explanation: The unemployment rate is a ratio, so it can rise even when jobs are created if the labour force grows faster — for example when improving conditions encourage discouraged workers to start job-hunting again and be counted as unemployed. Saying the figures must be wrong assumes more jobs must always cut the rate, which ignores movements in the denominator. Whenever a rate behaves oddly, check whether the denominator changed.

questions.stem: Economists warn against treating GDP per capita as a full measure of living standards. Which statement correctly identifies a limitation of GDP?
options: It counts unpaid volunteering and housework, so it overstates how much leisure households actually have
It rises only when income is shared more evenly, so it hides periods of strong overall growth
It automatically falls whenever pollution or resource depletion increases during the year
It measures market production, so it excludes unpaid household work and ignores how income is distributed
questions.explanation: GDP adds up production that passes through markets, so unpaid care and volunteering are left out, and an average per person says nothing about whether the gains reach most households. The option claiming GDP falls with pollution is the reverse of the truth: clean-up spending and resource extraction can actually add to measured GDP even as wellbeing suffers. Remember GDP counts market output only, and averages conceal distribution.

questions.stem: Over one year, an economy's nominal GDP rises by 4 per cent, the CPI rises by 3 per cent, and the population grows by 1.5 per cent. What does this suggest about material living standards?
options: Real GDP per person has fallen slightly, since real growth of about 1 per cent is less than population growth
Real GDP per person has risen by about 4 per cent, since nominal GDP grew faster than prices
Real GDP per person has risen by about 2.5 per cent, once population growth is subtracted from nominal growth
Real GDP per person is unchanged, because inflation and population growth cancel each other out
questions.explanation: To judge living standards you first remove inflation (4 per cent minus 3 per cent gives real growth of about 1 per cent), then compare that with population growth of 1.5 per cent — output per person has gone slightly backwards. The option claiming a rise of about 2.5 per cent subtracts population growth from the nominal figure and never adjusts for inflation, which is the most common slip. The order matters: nominal → real (subtract inflation) → per person (subtract population growth).

questions.stem: By value, Australia's largest single goods export in recent years has been:
options: Wheat
Refined petroleum
Iron ore
Motor vehicles
questions.explanation: Australia's export earnings are dominated by mineral resources, and iron ore has been the single largest goods export by value, sold mainly to steel producers in East Asia. Wheat is a significant agricultural export but is worth far less than iron ore each year. Motor vehicle manufacturing in Australia ceased in 2017, and refined petroleum is something Australia largely imports rather than exports.

questions.stem: Australia gradually removed most tariffs on imported motor vehicles in the decades before local car manufacturing ended in 2017. Which pair of outcomes best matches this change?
options: More tariff revenue for government and stronger protection for local vehicle manufacturers
Fewer imported models available to buyers and higher production costs for local vehicle manufacturers
Lower prices and more model choice for consumers, but job losses in local vehicle manufacturing
Higher prices and less model choice for consumers, but expanded employment in local vehicle manufacturing
questions.explanation: Cutting tariffs lowers the price of imported goods and widens consumer choice, but it also exposes import-competing local producers to competition, causing structural unemployment in those industries. The option pairing higher prices with expanded local employment is tempting because it sounds like the pre-tariff-cut world, but removing a tariff cannot raise import prices. Remember: tariffs raise import prices and protect local jobs, so removing them does the reverse.

questions.stem: A large share of Australia's exports goes to a single market, China. From an economic point of view, the main risk this concentration creates is that:
options: Australia would be permanently locked out of signing free trade agreements with other economies
Export prices would be fixed by that market, so Australian producers could no longer respond to global demand
A slowdown or trade restriction in that one market would have an outsized impact on Australian export income
Australian exchange rate movements would no longer affect the competitiveness of Australian exports
questions.explanation: Export concentration means the fortunes of many Australian industries, jobs and government revenues depend on demand in one economy, so a downturn or the imposition of trade barriers there transmits quickly to Australia. The option about the exchange rate is wrong because a falling or rising Australian dollar still changes the price foreign buyers pay, no matter who they are. Diversification of markets is the standard policy response to this risk.

questions.stem: Since the 1950s, where have Australia's exports gone? Which describes the shift?
options: Away from China and Japan towards the United States, now our largest export market
Away from the United Kingdom and Europe towards Asia, especially Japan and China
Away from Asian markets towards the United Kingdom and the European Union
Away from all overseas markets towards sales within Australia and New Zealand
questions.explanation: After the Second World War, and particularly after Britain joined the European Economic Community in 1973, Australia's trade reoriented towards Asia — first Japan, and from the 2000s China became by far the largest export market. The option naming the UK and EU as the growing destination reverses the actual direction of change; Britain's entry into the EEC reduced Australia's preferential access to that market. The cue is that geography plus rapid Asian industrialisation drew Australian resource exports north, not back to Europe.

questions.stem: Which of the following is one of Australia's largest services exports?
options: Imported machinery re-sold to Australian mining and farming businesses
Education-related travel, such as international students studying in Australia
Refined petroleum supplied to shipping fleets in the Pacific region
Passenger motor vehicles assembled in Australia for overseas buyers
questions.explanation: Services count as exports when they are sold to non-residents, and money spent in Australia by international students (education-related travel) is consistently one of Australia's biggest service export earners, alongside tourism. Motor vehicles are the tempting distractor, but Australian car assembly ended in 2017 and vehicles are now a major import, not an export. Remember that an export does not have to be shipped out — a foreign student paying fees and rent here earns Australia export income.

questions.stem: Which pair correctly identifies a benefit and a cost of globalisation for Australia?
options: Benefit: complete independence from overseas economic downturns; Cost: fewer choices for Australian consumers
Benefit: automatic elimination of income inequality; Cost: reduced access to foreign investment and technology
Benefit: cheaper imported consumer goods; Cost: job losses in industries exposed to lower-cost overseas competition
Benefit: guaranteed full employment in manufacturing; Cost: higher prices for imported clothing and electronics
questions.explanation: Globalisation lowers the price of many imported goods because they are produced where costs are lowest, but that same competition displaces workers in domestic industries such as clothing, footwear and vehicle assembly. The pairing of full employment in manufacturing with higher import prices is tempting because it mentions manufacturing, but both halves are false — open trade has reduced manufacturing employment and reduced import prices. Check each half of the pair separately: a pair is only correct if both statements are true.

questions.stem: A free trade agreement removes Australia's tariffs on imported processed food. Which combination of short-term effects is most likely?
options: Australian consumers pay less for the imported food, while some local food processors lose sales and cut staff
Australian consumers pay more for the imported food, while local food processors expand output and hire staff
Australian consumers pay less for the imported food, and local food processors also increase their market share
Australian consumers pay more for the imported food, and government tariff revenue from that food rises sharply
questions.explanation: A tariff is a tax on imports, so removing it lowers the landed price of the imported food, benefiting consumers but exposing domestic processors to stronger price competition, which can reduce their sales and employment. The option saying prices rise while local processors expand describes what happens when a tariff is imposed, not removed. The cue is direction: tariff off means import prices down and import-competing producers under more pressure.

questions.stem: The four elements of the traditional marketing mix are:
options: product, price, place and promotion
product, price, packaging and publicity
profit, price, place and promotion
product, production, place and promotion
questions.explanation: The classic marketing mix, or 4Ps, is product (what is sold), price (what is charged), place (how it reaches customers) and promotion (how it is communicated). The list containing 'packaging and publicity' is tempting because both are genuine marketing activities, but packaging sits within product and publicity within promotion — they are not separate elements of the mix. Remember that all four begin with P and each names a different decision the business must make.

questions.stem: Which action is the clearest example of entrepreneurship?
options: Reordering stock of a consistently bestselling item from the business's usual long-term supplier
Processing staff wages each fortnight using the payroll system the business already has in place
Checking the accounts at the end of the year to confirm the recorded figures are accurate
Identifying an unmet customer need, then investing personal savings to develop and launch a new product
questions.explanation: Entrepreneurship involves recognising an opportunity, organising resources and accepting personal financial risk to bring something new to the market. Reordering a bestselling item is routine management of an existing operation — it involves decisions but no new venture and no significant risk-taking. The cue is novelty plus risk: an entrepreneur creates something that did not exist before and stands to lose if it fails.

questions.stem: A small Australian coffee roaster charges well above supermarket prices, sources single-origin beans, and uses distinctive packaging and a story about its growers. This is best described as a strategy of:
options: market penetration through pricing below all rivals to win share quickly
exporting, selling the same product into several overseas markets at once
differentiation, making the product distinctive so buyers will pay a premium
cost leadership, producing at the lowest cost so it can undercut competitors
questions.explanation: Differentiation means building an advantage on qualities other than price — unique product features, branding, quality or story — so that customers accept a higher price. Cost leadership is tempting only if a student assumes every business competes on price, but this roaster is deliberately charging more, not less, so lowest-cost production is not the strategy. The cue is the direction of the price: premium pricing signals differentiation, low pricing signals cost leadership.

questions.stem: A sportswear company divides its customers into groups by age, income and activity type, then designs separate advertising campaigns for each group. This practice is called:
options: economies of scale
corporate takeover
market segmentation
vertical integration
questions.explanation: Market segmentation is dividing a broad market into smaller groups with shared characteristics so that promotion and product design can be targeted to each group. Vertical integration is tempting to students who remember it as a business growth strategy, but it means taking ownership of suppliers or distributors along the supply chain, which is not happening here. The cue is that segmentation is about splitting customers, while integration is about combining businesses.

questions.stem: Why is a strong brand reputation generally a more sustainable source of competitive advantage than a price cut?
options: A price cut always reduces total revenue, whereas building a reputation involves no cost to the business at all
Reputation can be purchased outright from an advertising agency, so it is more reliable than any pricing decision
Reputation is built over years and is difficult for rivals to imitate quickly, while a price cut can be matched within days
Businesses are legally prohibited from matching a competitor's advertised prices, but reputations may be freely copied
questions.explanation: An advantage is sustainable when rivals cannot easily copy it; brand trust accumulates slowly through consistent quality and communication, so competitors cannot replicate it overnight, whereas a price change can be matched almost immediately. The claim that firms are legally prohibited from matching prices is false — it is collusion to fix prices together, not independently matching them, that is illegal. The test to apply is simply: how fast and how cheaply could a competitor copy this?

questions.stem: A food manufacturer discovers a safety fault and must recall a product. From a public relations perspective, the most effective response is to:
options: say nothing publicly and wait for media interest in the fault to fade over coming weeks
launch a large advertising campaign for its other products to shift attention away from the recall
publicly blame the ingredient supplier and decline to offer refunds to affected customers
announce the recall promptly, explain the fault, apologise and set out how it will be fixed
questions.explanation: Effective crisis PR relies on speed, honesty and visible corrective action, because being open early preserves the trust that underpins the brand's long-term competitive advantage. Staying silent is tempting because it seems to avoid attention, but silence allows others to define the story and usually deepens the reputational damage when the facts emerge. The cue is that PR manages relationships and credibility over time, so short-term concealment almost always costs more than early disclosure.

questions.stem: An Australian supermarket chain invests heavily in automated distribution centres and buys in very large volumes, allowing it to sell everyday items for less than its rivals while still making a profit. This approach to competitive advantage is best described as:
options: Entrepreneurship, because reducing costs in an existing business is by definition the creation of a new venture
Cost leadership, because lower unit costs let the business undercut competitors' prices and still earn a margin
Product differentiation, because buying in bulk makes the chain's grocery items distinct from those of rivals
Market segmentation, because automated warehouses divide customers into separate groups with different needs
questions.explanation: Cost leadership means becoming the lowest-cost producer or seller in an industry, usually through economies of scale, technology and efficient supply chains, so the firm can compete on price and still be profitable. The tempting option is product differentiation, but bulk buying does not make the groceries different from those sold elsewhere — the products are the same, only cheaper. Ask what the customer is being offered: something distinctive (differentiation) or the same thing for less (cost leadership). Segmentation is about dividing a market into customer groups, and entrepreneurship involves taking risk to start or transform a venture, not routine efficiency gains.

questions.stem: According to Maslow's hierarchy of needs as applied to the workplace, a manager who provides safe equipment, secure ongoing contracts and clear safety procedures is mainly addressing employees':
options: Safety and security needs
Physiological needs
Esteem needs
Self-actualisation needs
questions.explanation: Maslow placed safety and security — physical safety at work and job security — on the second level of the hierarchy, and safe equipment and secure contracts sit squarely there. Physiological needs is the tempting choice because safety sounds basic, but that level is about survival needs such as food, water and rest, which in a workplace are met by wages and adequate breaks. The cue is that physiological needs are about the body's survival, while safety needs are about protection from harm and uncertainty.

questions.stem: Human resource management in a business is best described as:
options: managing the recruitment, development, wellbeing and performance of a business's employees
managing the purchase, storage and use of a business's raw materials and equipment
managing the recording, auditing and reporting of a business's financial transactions
managing the advertising, pricing and distribution of a business's products
questions.explanation: HRM is the management function concerned with people: attracting, hiring, training, motivating, rewarding and retaining staff, and looking after their wellbeing and performance. Managing raw materials and equipment is operations management, not HRM, even though both affect productivity. The cue is the word 'human' — if the resource being managed is not people, it is a different business function.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a non-financial motivator used by employers?
options: Paying an employee a bonus when quarterly sales targets are exceeded
Increasing an employee's hourly base rate after a performance review
Offering employees additional superannuation contributions above the legal minimum
Giving an employee greater responsibility and the chance to lead a project
questions.explanation: Non-financial motivators meet needs such as recognition, achievement and responsibility rather than adding to an employee's pay or benefits. Extra superannuation contributions are tempting because no cash is handed over immediately, but super is still money paid on the employee's behalf, so it is a financial reward. Ask whether the reward increases what the worker is paid — if yes, it is financial.

questions.stem: A café loses a third of its staff every year, and the owner constantly pays for advertising, interviews and retraining. High staff turnover most directly reduces the café's competitiveness because:
options: the wages paid to remaining employees must legally be increased to compensate them
turnover automatically breaches the National Employment Standards, exposing the business to fines
the business is required to raise its prices whenever it advertises a vacancy
recruitment and training costs rise while less experienced staff serve customers more slowly
questions.explanation: Turnover imposes direct costs (advertising, interviewing, inducting, training) and indirect costs, because new staff take time to reach the speed and service quality of experienced workers, hurting both costs and customer satisfaction. The claim that remaining employees must legally receive higher wages is false — no law compensates staff for colleagues resigning. Look for cost and productivity effects, not invented legal obligations.

questions.stem: A logistics firm introduces flexible start times and a option to work from home two days a week for office staff. From an HRM perspective, the most likely business benefit is:
options: improved retention and morale, helping the firm attract skilled staff its rivals struggle to keep
a legally guaranteed rise in output, because flexible hours increase every worker's productivity
lower wage costs, because employees working from home may be paid below the award rate
the removal of the firm's work health and safety duties for staff working at home
questions.explanation: Flexible work is a non-financial strategy that helps employees balance work and life, which typically lifts morale and retention and makes the employer more attractive in a competitive labour market. The claim about a guaranteed productivity rise is wrong because flexibility affects individuals differently and no such guarantee exists. Employers also keep WHS duties for employees working at home, and award rates apply regardless of work location.

questions.stem: Two competing warehouses pay identical wages. One has far higher productivity and lower absenteeism. Which explanation best shows how HRM, rather than pay, created this competitive advantage?
options: It hires only casual employees, so shifts can be cancelled whenever demand falls unexpectedly
It invests in ongoing training, recognition of good work and consulting staff about how tasks are organised
It employs more staff overall, so each shift always has extra workers available on the floor
It sets faster targets and monitors every worker closely, removing their input into how work is done
questions.explanation: Where financial rewards are the same, differences in performance usually come from non-financial strategies: skills built through training, recognition that satisfies esteem needs, and job design or consultation that gives workers some control, all of which raise engagement and lower absenteeism. Tight monitoring with no employee input is the tempting opposite — it may lift short-term output but typically increases stress, dissatisfaction and absence. Simply employing more staff raises wage costs and does not improve productivity per worker.

questions.stem: A new employee's first day covers a site tour, safety, the team and values. This is:
options: Performance appraisal, reviewing work against agreed standards
Separation, managing the ending of the employment relationship
Induction, settling a new employee into the role, procedures and culture
Recruitment, attracting and selecting the best applicant for a vacancy
questions.explanation: Induction (or onboarding) is the HRM stage that follows selection: it orients a newly hired worker to their duties, workplace procedures, safety requirements and the culture of the business so they become productive sooner. Recruitment is the tempting choice because it also involves new staff, but recruitment happens before the person is hired — it is the attracting and selecting stage, and the scenario describes someone who already has the job. The cue is timing: before an offer it is recruitment and selection; after the person starts it is induction.

questions.stem: The peak national body representing trade unions in Australia is the:
options: Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC)
Australian Industry Group (Ai Group)
Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS)
Australian Council of Trade Unions (ACTU)
questions.explanation: The ACTU is the peak council to which most Australian trade unions are affiliated, and it speaks for unions in national wage cases and public debate. The Australian Industry Group is the tempting swap, but it is a peak employer association representing businesses, not workers. Remember that 'Council of Trade Unions' names its members directly.

questions.stem: Nurses at a private hospital ask their union to meet management to negotiate a new agreement covering wages, rosters and staffing ratios for all nursing staff. This process is best described as:
options: market segmentation
collective bargaining
performance appraisal
industrial action
questions.explanation: Collective bargaining is where employees, usually through a union, negotiate terms and conditions as a group rather than individually, producing an enterprise agreement. Industrial action is tempting, but that refers to steps such as strikes or work bans used to apply pressure, not to the negotiation itself. The cue: bargaining is talking at the table, industrial action is what may happen if talking stalls.

questions.stem: A trade union is:
options: a government body setting the minimum wage and ruling on dismissals
an association of business owners lobbying on behalf of employers
a department inside a business handling recruitment and training
an organisation of workers representing members on pay and conditions
questions.explanation: A union is a members' organisation formed by employees who pool their numbers so they can bargain and advocate collectively rather than one at a time. The option describing a body that sets the minimum wage and rules on dismissals is the Fair Work Commission, an independent tribunal, not a union. The cue is who the organisation is made up of and who pays its fees: unions are funded by and answerable to worker members, while employer associations are funded by businesses.

questions.stem: What is the main role of an employer association such as the Australian Industry Group?
options: inspecting workplaces and prosecuting breaches of health and safety law
representing and advising member businesses, and lobbying on their behalf
representing individual employees in disputes with management over pay
setting the national minimum wage and award conditions each year
questions.explanation: Employer associations are membership bodies funded by businesses; they give members industrial relations advice, represent them in bargaining and tribunals, and put the employer view to government. Representing individual employees in disputes is the role of a union, which is the mirror image of an employer group. Minimum wages and awards are set by the Fair Work Commission, and safety enforcement belongs to state and territory regulators such as WorkSafe.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a peak body representing employers in Australia?
options: the Australian Bureau of Statistics
the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry
the Australian Council of Trade Unions
the Fair Work Ombudsman
questions.explanation: The correct choice is the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry, a national peak body whose members are business and industry associations. The Australian Council of Trade Unions is the peak body on the other side of the table, representing affiliated unions and their worker members. The Fair Work Ombudsman is a government agency that provides information and enforces workplace laws, and the Australian Bureau of Statistics collects national data.

questions.stem: A warehouse worker is called to a meeting where management will discuss allegations about her conduct. She asks her union delegate to attend with her. In this situation the delegate's role is to:
options: support and speak for the member, making sure the correct procedure and her rights are followed
decide whether the allegations are proven and whether any penalty should apply to her
negotiate a new enterprise agreement covering pay and rosters for the whole warehouse
order the business to stop the meeting until the Fair Work Commission has investigated
questions.explanation: One of the everyday roles of a union is individual representation: a delegate or organiser accompanies a member to disciplinary or grievance meetings to advocate for them and check that agreed procedures are followed. The option about deciding whether the allegations are proven is wrong because the delegate is an advocate, not an umpire — only the employer decides at that stage, and disputed outcomes go to the Fair Work Commission. Ask yourself whether the union is speaking for someone or judging them; unions always do the former.

questions.stem: Union membership in Australia has fallen from around 40 per cent of employees in the early 1990s to well under 15 per cent today. A likely consequence of this trend in workplaces is that:
options: unions have less collective bargaining strength, and more pay is set by individual arrangements
modern awards no longer legally apply, so employers set all pay and conditions themselves
employer associations have declined at the same rate, leaving no peak bodies for business
the Fair Work Commission has taken over the negotiation of every enterprise agreement
questions.explanation: A union's leverage comes largely from the proportion of a workforce it represents, so falling density weakens its bargaining position and shifts more wage setting to individual contracts and employer-determined pay. The claim that awards no longer apply is false: modern awards remain legally binding minimum standards regardless of whether workers are union members. Separate the strength of an organisation from the existence of legal minimums — the second does not depend on the first.

questions.stem: Each year the Fair Work Commission conducts a review of the national minimum wage, and both the ACTU and employer groups such as the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry lodge submissions. Which statement best describes the typical roles of these two organisations in that process?
options: Unions and employer groups negotiate the new minimum wage directly with each other, and the Commission simply records the figure the two sides agree on
Unions argue for a larger increase, pointing to living costs for low-paid workers, while employer groups argue for a smaller rise, pointing to labour costs and jobs
Employer groups argue for a larger increase, pointing to worker retention, while unions argue for a smaller rise, pointing to the risk of job losses among members
Employer groups decide the size of the increase, while unions may only advise the Commission on how it should be phased in for low-paid workers
questions.explanation: Trade unions exist to advance employees' pay and conditions, so in wage reviews they press for the largest increase they can justify on cost-of-living grounds; employer associations represent business owners' interests and typically warn that large increases raise wage costs and may reduce hiring. The decision itself is made by the Fair Work Commission, an independent umpire, after considering both submissions. The option that has the two sides negotiating the wage directly is tempting because unions and employer groups do bargain directly in other settings, but the national minimum wage is set by the Commission, not by agreement between the parties. Cue: unions push wages up, employer groups push back, and an independent body decides.

questions.stem: How are risk and expected return related when investing?
options: Investments with higher expected returns generally carry greater risk of loss
Investments with higher expected returns carry lower risk, as only good providers offer them
Risk and return are unrelated; return depends only on how long money is invested
All investments from Australian banks carry the same low risk, set by law
questions.explanation: The risk-return trade-off is the core principle of investing: investors will only accept a higher chance of loss if they are compensated with the prospect of a higher return, so safe products like term deposits pay less than shares. The tempting wrong answer is that high returns come from low-risk, reputable providers — in fact, promises of high returns with 'no risk' are a classic warning sign of a scam. Time invested affects how much compounding occurs, but it does not remove the link between risk and return.

questions.stem: Three weeks after buying a laptop, Sam finds it shuts down randomly and cannot be reliably used. The retailer says he must deal with the manufacturer because he did not buy the extended warranty. Under Australian Consumer Law, which statement is correct?
options: Sam can only claim within a 7-day cooling-off period, which has already expired for this purchase
The retailer must deal with the claim, and for a major failure Sam can choose a refund or replacement
The retailer is correct: once goods are sold, responsibility passes to the manufacturer's warranty
Sam has no claim, because consumer guarantees apply only if an extended warranty was purchased
questions.explanation: Consumer guarantees under the Australian Consumer Law apply automatically to the seller and cannot be excluded; where the failure is major, the consumer chooses between a refund and a replacement. The tempting answer is that responsibility shifts to the manufacturer, but a manufacturer's warranty is an extra promise that sits alongside — not instead of — the retailer's legal obligations. Extended warranties are optional add-ons, and there is no general 7-day cooling-off period for ordinary in-store purchases.

questions.stem: After losing $8,000 to a fake online investment platform, Marco is phoned by a 'fund recovery service' that says it can retrieve his money for an upfront fee of $600 plus his bank login details. The best analysis is:
options: This is a follow-up recovery scam; he should pay nothing, report it and contact his bank about the original loss
It is a legitimate service, because recovery firms must charge upfront to cover the cost of legal action
It is safe to proceed since he has already lost the money, so the $600 fee is the only remaining risk
It is genuine if the caller can quote the exact amount he lost, as only official investigators hold that information
questions.explanation: Scam victims' details are often resold, and a second wave of scammers targets them with promises of recovery in exchange for an upfront fee or account access — a well-documented pattern reported to Scamwatch. The most tempting distractor is that the $600 is the only remaining risk, but handing over bank login details exposes every account he holds, not just the fee. Genuine action starts with his own bank and official reporting channels, and knowing the amount lost proves nothing because the original scammers hold that data.

questions.stem: In an insurance policy, the 'excess' is best described as:
options: the extra cover a policyholder buys for items worth more than the standard limit
the amount the policyholder must pay towards a claim before the insurer pays the rest
the regular amount the policyholder pays the insurer to keep the policy active
the maximum total amount the insurer will pay out for any single claim
questions.explanation: An excess is the policyholder's own contribution to each claim; the insurer covers the balance up to the sum insured, and choosing a higher excess usually lowers the premium. The option describing a regular payment to keep the policy active defines the premium, not the excess — the two are easily swapped because both involve money paid by the customer. The cue is timing: a premium is paid to hold the policy, an excess is paid only when you claim.

questions.stem: An adviser tells a client to 'diversify'. This means the client should:
options: choose only investments guaranteed by the government against loss
spread money across different assets so one poor performer matters less
move all savings into the asset class with the highest return last year
hold one investment as long as possible so returns can build up
questions.explanation: Diversification manages risk by holding a mix of assets whose values do not all rise and fall together, so a loss in one part of a portfolio can be offset elsewhere. Holding an investment for a long time describes a long-term strategy, not diversification — both are sensible strategies, which is why they get mixed up. Remember diversification is about spreading across investments, not about time.

questions.stem: Priya gets an unexpected text saying her electricity account is overdue and will be cut off within two hours unless she pays through a link, using gift card codes. The strongest indicators that this is a scam are:
options: the amount claimed being small enough that most people would pay it without checking
the message referring to her electricity account rather than naming her retailer's plan
the unsolicited contact, the extreme urgency and the demand for payment by gift cards
the fact that it arrived by text message rather than by a posted paper bill
questions.explanation: Classic scam markers are contact you did not initiate, artificial time pressure that stops you checking, and payment methods that are hard to trace or reverse, such as gift cards or crypto. The option about it arriving by text is tempting, but legitimate retailers do send account texts, so the delivery channel alone proves nothing. Focus on the combination of pressure plus an unusual payment method, not the medium used.

questions.stem: Dylan is a self-employed electrician with a mortgage. He wants cover that will replace part of his regular earnings if illness or injury stops him working for several months. The most suitable type of insurance is:
options: compulsory third party insurance
home and contents insurance
comprehensive vehicle insurance
income protection insurance
questions.explanation: Income protection pays a proportion of a person's usual earnings for a set period while they are unable to work due to illness or injury, which is exactly the risk Dylan faces. Compulsory third party insurance is tempting because it also involves injury, but it covers injuries caused to other people in a motor vehicle accident, not the policyholder's lost wages. Ask what is being insured: here it is future earnings, not property or liability to others.

questions.stem: When applying for home insurance, Marcus does not mention that the house has previously been flooded, because he thinks it will raise his premium. A flood later damages the home and he lodges a claim. The best analysis of his position is:
options: the insurer must pay in full, because it had the chance to inspect the property before insuring it
the claim must be paid but the insurer can charge him a higher premium for the following year
the contract is automatically void, so he can only recover the premiums he has already paid
he has breached his duty of disclosure, so the insurer may lawfully reduce or refuse the claim
questions.explanation: Insurance contracts require applicants to disclose matters relevant to the insurer's decision to offer cover and set a price; failing to do so can allow the insurer to reduce a payout or decline the claim altogether. The idea that the insurer must pay because it could have inspected the property is tempting but wrong — the legal obligation to disclose known risks sits with the applicant. The cue is that the insurer prices the risk using information only the applicant holds, so honesty is both a legal duty and an ethical one.

questions.stem: Jarrah has changed jobs four times and now has four separate super accounts, each with a small balance. Why do financial advisers generally recommend he consolidate them into one fund?
options: Consolidating is required by law, because a worker is permitted to hold only one superannuation account at any time
Each account charges its own administration fees and may deduct separate insurance premiums, which erodes small balances over time
Holding several accounts means his employer must split the compulsory contribution, so each account receives less than the required rate
Combining accounts adds the returns of all four funds together, which guarantees him a higher overall rate of return
questions.explanation: Fees and insurance premiums are charged per account, so multiple small balances can be steadily eaten away by duplicated costs — consolidating leaves one set of fees. The claim that combining accounts adds returns together misunderstands how returns work: a percentage return applies to the balance, so merging changes the fees, not the rate. Check for duplicate insurance cover as well as fees when comparing accounts.

questions.stem: On average, Australian women retire with lower superannuation balances than men. Which explanation of this gap is economically accurate?
options: Superannuation funds are permitted to apply a lower rate of investment return to accounts held by women than to those held by men
Part-time and casual employees are excluded from the Superannuation Guarantee, so no contributions are made for them at all
Employers are legally required to pay the Superannuation Guarantee during all periods of unpaid parental leave, which offsets the difference
Time out of paid work and more part-time hours reduce contributions, and those missed contributions also lose years of compounding returns
questions.explanation: Because super is a percentage of earnings, lower lifetime earnings from career breaks and part-time work mean fewer and smaller contributions, and each missed contribution also forgoes decades of compound growth. The claim that part-time and casual employees are excluded is false — the Superannuation Guarantee applies to employees regardless of hours, with only limited exceptions such as some under-18 workers. Trace the gap back to earnings and time, not to different treatment by funds.

questions.stem: Under the Superannuation Guarantee, who must make super contributions for an employee?
options: The employee, who must have a set percentage deducted from their pay
The federal government, which deposits a set amount into each fund yearly
The super fund, which credits members a percentage of their balance yearly
The employer, who must pay a set percentage of ordinary time earnings
questions.explanation: The Superannuation Guarantee places the legal obligation on employers: they must pay a percentage of an eligible employee's ordinary time earnings into a complying fund, on top of wages. The idea that it is deducted from take-home pay is the most common misunderstanding — employees may choose to add extra through salary sacrifice or personal contributions, but the guarantee itself is an employer cost. The cue is the word 'guarantee': it guarantees employer-funded contributions, not employee deductions.

questions.stem: Two workers each contribute the same total amount to super over their careers. Mia's contributions are made mostly in her twenties and thirties; Tom's are made mostly in his fifties. Why is Mia likely to retire with a larger balance?
options: Funds charge no administration or insurance fees on accounts belonging to members who are under 40 years of age
Her contributions spend longer invested, so earnings are reinvested and themselves earn returns over many more years
Super funds are required to pay a higher rate of return on contributions made by members under the age of 40
Contributions made before age 40 are exempt from all tax, while later contributions are taxed at the member's full marginal rate
questions.explanation: Compounding is the key: earnings are added to the balance and then generate further earnings, so money invested early has far more time to grow. The claim that early contributions are tax-free is wrong — concessional contributions are generally taxed at 15 per cent regardless of the member's age. The cue is time in the market, not the member's age itself, doing the work.

questions.stem: Leila earns $95,000 and arranges to salary sacrifice $5,000 a year into super. Ignoring caps and fees, what is the main financial advantage of doing this rather than taking the $5,000 as wages?
options: Her employer must match the sacrificed amount dollar for dollar, doubling the contribution made to her account that year
The sacrificed amount can be withdrawn at any time without tax, which makes it more flexible than money kept in her bank account
The sacrificed amount is generally taxed at 15 per cent going into the fund instead of at her higher marginal income tax rate
The sacrificed amount is completely free of tax both when it enters the fund and when it is later withdrawn at any age
questions.explanation: Salary sacrificed (concessional) contributions are generally taxed at 15 per cent when they enter the fund, which is below the marginal tax rate applying to a $95,000 income, so more of the money is invested. The 'completely free of tax' option is tempting because super is taxed lightly, but contributions tax still applies. The trade-off to remember is that the tax saving comes at the cost of preservation: the money is locked away until a condition of release is met.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most suitable inquiry question for a Year 10 investigation of a contemporary economic issue?
options: What is the single best interest rate for the Australian economy to have?
How have rising interest rates since 2022 affected household spending in Australia?
Are high interest rates bad for people who live in Australia today?
Did the Reserve Bank of Australia raise the cash rate in 2022, yes or no?
questions.explanation: A workable inquiry question is open, focused on a specific issue, and answerable using evidence such as spending and inflation data over a stated time period. Asking whether high interest rates are 'bad' is a value judgement with no agreed evidence base, so different sources could never settle it. Asking whether the cash rate rose is a closed factual check answered in one word, and asking for the 'single best' rate calls for an opinion no data can confirm. Cue: a good question needs scope (who, where, when) and can be answered with evidence, not a yes or a personal preference.

questions.stem: In an economics or business investigation, a 'closed' question is one that:
options: requires the researcher to gather data from more than one source
cannot be answered because the necessary information is confidential
asks about the future rather than about the past or the present
can be answered with a single fact, a number or a yes/no response
questions.explanation: Closed questions have a limited, definite answer such as a figure, a date or yes/no, so they are useful for gathering background facts but too narrow to structure a whole investigation. The option about needing several sources describes an open inquiry question, which is the opposite of closed. Being confidential makes a question impractical, not closed, and questions about the future can be either open or closed. Cue: 'closed' describes the range of possible answers, not the difficulty or timeframe.

questions.stem: Why do researchers often modify their inquiry question part-way through an investigation?
options: Because a question must be changed until it answers yes or no
Because it should be reworded to match the conclusion preferred
Because modifying it removes the need to collect further evidence
Because early research reveals what data exists, so it can be sharpened
questions.explanation: Questions are modified in response to what the first round of sources shows: the topic may be too broad, or the data may only cover certain years, regions or industries, so the question is narrowed or refocused. Rewording a question to match a preferred conclusion is the opposite of good practice, since it builds bias into the inquiry. Narrowing to a yes/no answer makes the question weaker, and no rewording removes the need for evidence. Cue: modification is driven by the evidence available, never by the answer you hope to find.

questions.stem: Which question is unsuitable for an evidence-based investigation because it asks only for a value judgement?
options: Should Australians care more about the environment than about jobs?
How many Australians were employed in renewable energy in 2023?
What effect did the closure of a coal-fired power station have on local employment?
How have job numbers in Australian coal mining changed over the past decade?
questions.explanation: A question asking what people 'should' care about more sets up a clash of values, and no set of statistics can establish which value ought to win. The other three each name a measurable quantity or a traceable effect, so employment data, regional labour force figures and industry statistics can answer them. The employment-effect question is the most tempting distractor because it sounds debatable, but it asks what did happen to jobs, which is measurable. Cue: words like 'should' or 'more important' signal a values question rather than a researchable one.

questions.stem: A student begins with the question 'Why is the cost of living so bad?' Which is the best modification for a school investigation?
options: Is the cost of living in Australia bad, or is it actually fine at the moment?
Why do governments and businesses refuse to fix the cost-of-living problem?
What is the total amount every Australian household spent on all items last year?
Which household costs rose fastest in Victoria between 2021 and 2024, and why?
questions.explanation: The original question is vague and assumes a judgement, so the improvement adds a place, a time period and a measurable focus (which costs rose fastest) plus a causal element. Asking whether the cost of living 'is bad or fine' keeps the value judgement and reduces the question to a two-way choice. The 'refuse to fix' version smuggles in an unproven assumption, and the total-spending question asks for one enormous figure that produces no analysis. Cue: sharpen by adding scope and a measurable variable, not by adding an accusation.

questions.stem: A student wants to investigate youth unemployment but finds that reliable published data is only available by state and by broad age group. The best response is to:
options: reword the question to compare youth unemployment across states over a set period
keep the original wording and estimate the missing local figures from personal experience
abandon the topic entirely because no perfect local data set has been published
survey twelve classmates and present the results as the youth unemployment rate
questions.explanation: Modifying a question so its scope matches the data that genuinely exists is a core research skill: shifting from suburb-level to state-level comparison keeps the inquiry rigorous. Estimating missing figures from personal experience invents data and destroys the reliability of the findings. Abandoning a workable topic is unnecessary when the question can be rescoped, and a class of twelve is far too small and unrepresentative to produce an unemployment rate. Cue: reshape the question around available evidence rather than manufacturing evidence to fit the question.

questions.stem: A student proposes: 'Why do greedy supermarkets rip off Australian farmers?' The main methodological problem with this question is that it:
options: is too narrow, because it names only one industry and one country
cannot be researched, as no information about supermarket pricing is published
concerns a business issue rather than an economic issue, so it is off-topic
assumes its own conclusion, so the research can only confirm a preset view
questions.explanation: The wording builds in the judgements that supermarkets are greedy and that farmers are being ripped off, so any evidence collected is likely to be selected to fit that assumption; a neutral version would ask how farmgate prices compare with retail prices and why. Calling it 'too narrow' is wrong, since naming an industry and a country is exactly the kind of scope a good question needs. Supermarket and farmgate price information is published by regulators and industry bodies, and supply chains sit comfortably within economics and business. Cue: check whether the question's wording already decides the answer.

questions.stem: In an economics investigation, which of the following would be classified as a primary source of data?
options: A textbook chapter explaining how the labour market works
A survey of 120 local shoppers designed and conducted by the student
A media release published on the Reserve Bank of Australia website
A newspaper article summarising the latest unemployment figures
questions.explanation: A primary source is data the researcher gathers first-hand for their own purpose, such as their own survey, interview or observation. The Reserve Bank media release is tempting because the RBA is an original, authoritative body, but for the student it is still material produced by someone else and interpreted before it reached them, making it secondary. The cue is who collected the data: if the student collected it themselves, it is primary.

questions.stem: You need current, reliable data on Australia's unemployment rate. Which source?
options: An opinion column in a newspaper arguing that job losses are worsening
A forum thread where job seekers describe their own experiences
The Australian Bureau of Statistics, which publishes the Labour Force Survey
A recruitment firm's blog summarising the job ads on its own website
questions.explanation: The ABS is Australia's official statistical agency and its Labour Force Survey is the source of the headline unemployment rate, collected using a consistent national sampling method. The recruitment company's blog is tempting because it does contain job market information, but it only covers ads on one commercial site, so it is not a measure of national unemployment and the company has an interest in presenting a positive picture. The cue is to ask who collected the data, how widely, and whether they benefit from a particular result.

questions.stem: A striking statistic appears on a social media infographic with no author, date or source. What next?
options: Trace the figure back to the organisation that produced it and check the date
Include it in the report and note that it came from social media
Discard it and avoid using any statistics found online at all
Include it only if two other social media posts show the same number
questions.explanation: Selecting information responsibly means verifying where a figure came from and when it was produced, because undated or unattributed data may be wrong, out of date or taken out of context. Citing it as 'from social media' is tempting because it looks like honest referencing, but naming the platform does not establish who collected the data or whether it is accurate. The cue is that a source is only checked once you can name the organisation, the method and the year.

questions.stem: To investigate how young Australians spend their income, a student surveys 25 classmates at her school during lunchtime. What is the main limitation of this data?
options: The sample is drawn from one school, so it may not represent young Australians generally
The sample is too recent, so the results will be out of date within a year
Survey data cannot be used in economics investigations because it is not official
The results cannot be graphed because responses about spending are opinions
questions.explanation: A sample of 25 students from one school shares a location, age range and socioeconomic setting, so the findings cannot be generalised to all young Australians even if the survey itself is well written. The claim that survey data cannot be used is a common misreading: student-collected surveys are legitimate primary data, provided their limitations are stated. The cue is to ask who was left out of the sample before judging what the results can prove.

questions.stem: A student's data shows that over five years, the number of cafés in a suburb rose and average house prices in that suburb also rose. Which conclusion is properly supported by this data alone?
options: The two variables moved in the same direction over the period, but a cause has not been shown
New cafés caused house prices to rise by making the suburb more attractive to buyers
Rising house prices caused more cafés to open by increasing local spending power
The data is unusable because two variables cannot be compared over the same period
questions.explanation: Two variables rising together is a correlation; establishing cause requires evidence about the mechanism and ruling out other factors, such as population growth driving both. Both causal options sound plausible and each names a believable mechanism, but the data given contains no evidence about which change came first or why, so neither is supported. The cue is that a claim beginning 'caused' needs more than two lines moving together.

questions.stem: A student reports that in one suburb the mean (average) annual income is $128,000 while the median is $71,000. What does this gap most likely indicate?
options: Incomes in the suburb are evenly spread, since the mean and median differ only slightly
The mean is always the more accurate measure, so the median should be left out
A small number of very high incomes are pulling the mean above the typical income
Most residents earn close to $128,000, and the median has been calculated incorrectly
questions.explanation: The mean is affected by extreme values while the median is the middle value, so a mean well above the median signals a right-skewed distribution with some very high earners. Assuming the median must be miscalculated is the tempting error, but the two measures are meant to differ when data is skewed; the gap is information, not a mistake. When reporting income data, the median usually describes the typical resident better.

questions.stem: A report states that Australia's annual inflation rate fell from 6 per cent to 4 per cent. The most accurate way to describe this change is that inflation:
options: fell by 2 percentage points, and prices on average were still rising, just more slowly
fell by 2 per cent, which means average prices were 2 per cent lower than a year earlier
fell to zero growth, because a lower inflation rate means prices have stopped rising
fell by 33 per cent, which means average prices dropped by one third over the year
questions.explanation: A move from 6 per cent to 4 per cent is a fall of 2 percentage points, and because the rate is still positive, the price level is continuing to rise — just at a slower pace (disinflation, not deflation). The option saying prices were 2 per cent lower confuses a change in the rate with a change in the price level. The cue: subtracting one percentage figure from another gives percentage points, and prices only fall when the inflation rate is negative.

questions.stem: A suburban café owner notices revenue dropping over six months, a period in which the Reserve Bank raised the cash rate several times. The most economically sound cause-and-effect explanation is that:
options: higher interest rates raised mortgage repayments, leaving households less discretionary income to spend on eating out
higher interest rates increased households' disposable income, so customers chose to save rather than spend it
higher interest rates directly cut the café's wage bill, which reduced the amount of revenue it recorded
higher interest rates raised menu prices automatically, which is what caused revenue to be recorded as lower
questions.explanation: Rate rises increase repayments for borrowers, squeezing discretionary spending, and eating out is one of the first categories households cut — a clear causal chain from policy to spending to café revenue. The option claiming disposable income rose is the reverse of the actual effect for mortgage holders; higher repayments reduce, not raise, income available to spend. A useful cue is to trace each step of the chain and check the direction of each arrow.

questions.stem: A hardware business reports that its sales revenue rose 3 per cent over the year, while the prices it charges rose 5 per cent over the same period. The best analysis of this data is that:
options: in real terms revenue fell, so the business most likely sold a smaller quantity of goods than the year before
in real terms revenue rose by 8 per cent, because price rises and revenue rises are added together
the business sold 3 per cent more goods, because a rise in revenue always means a rise in quantity sold
the price data is irrelevant to revenue analysis, since revenue is measured in dollars rather than quantities
questions.explanation: Revenue equals price times quantity, so if prices rose faster than revenue, the quantity sold must have fallen — revenue went backwards in real terms. The option claiming the business sold 3 per cent more goods is tempting because it reads the headline figure directly, but that figure is inflated by higher prices, not more sales. The cue is to always ask whether a dollar figure is nominal or has been adjusted for price changes.

questions.stem: House prices in a regional town rose about 10 per cent in each of the past three years. A student concludes that prices will rise 10 per cent again next year. The strongest evaluation of this reasoning is that:
