options: extrapolating a short trend ignores the conditions driving it, such as interest rates and supply, which may change
a trend observed over three consecutive years is long enough to make the prediction statistically certain
past data can never be used to inform predictions, so any forecast from historical figures is invalid
prices must fall next year, because a market that has risen for three years is always due for a correction
questions.explanation: Forecasts based on trends only hold while the causes behind the trend persist, so the student needs to examine drivers such as interest rates, population change and new housing supply before projecting forward. The claim that three years makes the prediction certain is tempting because the pattern looks consistent, but consistency in the past does not guarantee the underlying conditions continue. Equally, the idea that a rise 'must' be followed by a fall is a gambler's-fallacy style rule, not economics.

questions.stem: In an economics investigation, a 'trend' in a set of data is best described as:
options: the general direction in which the figures move over a period of time
the highest figure recorded in the data set during the period
the difference between the largest and the smallest figures recorded
a single unusual figure that does not fit the rest of the data
questions.explanation: A trend is the overall direction of movement (rising, falling or steady) shown by data across several time periods, which is why one year's change alone is not a trend. The option naming the difference between the largest and smallest figures describes the range, a measure of spread rather than direction. An unusual figure that does not fit is an outlier or anomaly. Cue: a trend always needs several time periods, not one point.

questions.stem: When Australia's unemployment rate is reported each month, it measures the percentage of:
options: people currently receiving government unemployment payments
the labour force who are without work and actively looking for work
the total Australian population who do not currently have a paid job
working-age adults who are not in full-time paid employment
questions.explanation: The unemployment rate uses the labour force (people employed plus people unemployed and actively seeking work) as its base, so people not looking for work are outside the calculation entirely. The option about all working-age adults without full-time work is tempting but wrong, because part-time workers count as employed and retirees, students and carers who are not job-hunting are not in the labour force. Cue: to be counted as unemployed a person must be both without work and actively searching.

questions.stem: A café's data shows that over one year its sales revenue rose from $40,000 to $44,000 a month, while its total monthly costs rose from $30,000 to $36,000. The most accurate analysis of this data is that the business:
options: is making a loss, because its costs rose by more dollars than its revenue did
has kept profit steady, since revenue and costs both increased over the year
is growing in revenue but its monthly profit has fallen from $10,000 to $8,000
is growing strongly, because revenue rose by $4,000 and profit must also have risen
questions.explanation: Profit is revenue minus costs, so profit moved from $10,000 to $8,000 even though revenue increased; costs grew 20 per cent while revenue grew only 10 per cent. The claim that the business is making a loss is wrong because revenue still exceeds costs — a smaller profit is not a loss. Cue: always subtract, and compare percentage growth rates, before judging performance from a revenue figure alone.

questions.stem: When drawing a conclusion from data, a student should make sure it:
options: states only what the evidence shows, without extending past what was measured
is expressed strongly, because hedged conclusions look like weak analysis
includes a prediction about the future, since data is collected to forecast
matches the view of the organisation that published the data
questions.explanation: A logical conclusion is one the evidence supports; claims that go past what was measured are unsupported, even if they sound reasonable. The idea that a conclusion must be stated strongly confuses confidence with validity — overstating certainty is a reasoning error, not good analysis. Data can support cautious forecasts, but a conclusion is not required to predict the future, and predictions based on short data sets are often unreliable. Test each sentence of a conclusion by asking which piece of data proves it.

questions.stem: Why cross-check an economic statistic against a second, independent source?
options: Because averaging two published figures always gives a better estimate
To make the report longer, since markers credit the number of sources
To confirm the figure was not mis-stated or taken out of context
Because a statistic is only valid if two organisations have published it
questions.explanation: Cross-checking tests whether a figure has been copied incorrectly, quoted without its definition or time period, or spun to suit an argument. The claim that a statistic is only valid if two organisations publish it is false — the Australian Bureau of Statistics is often the sole producer of a series, and that data is still valid. Averaging two figures that measure different things or different periods makes the estimate worse, not better. The cue is that cross-checking is about testing accuracy and context, not counting sources.

questions.stem: A student finds a column graph of a supermarket's quarterly profit where the vertical axis starts at $480 million rather than zero, making the columns look dramatically different. The most logical response is to:
options: read the actual values on the axis and calculate the percentage change before drawing a conclusion
reject the graph entirely, because a graph with a truncated axis contains falsified data
conclude that profit rose sharply, since the visual difference between the columns is large
redraw the graph as a line graph, which removes the distortion caused by the axis scale
questions.explanation: A truncated axis exaggerates visual differences but does not change the underlying figures, so the sound approach is to work with the numbers and express the change as a percentage. Rejecting the graph as falsified is wrong: the data may be perfectly accurate and from a verified source, only the presentation is misleading. Concluding profit rose sharply from the look of the columns is exactly the error the scale invites. Switching to a line graph changes nothing, because the same truncated scale would still apply.

questions.stem: A student finds a report concluding that a proposed tax on sugary drinks would cost thousands of jobs. The report is well presented and uses real ABS data, but was commissioned and funded by a beverage industry association. The soundest approach is to:
options: use the report but state who funded it, and compare its findings with independent research
exclude the report, because research funded by an interested party cannot contain valid data
accept the findings without qualification, since the report draws on official ABS statistics
include the report only in a section on opinions, as funded research is not evidence
questions.explanation: Funding creates a potential conflict of interest that may shape which questions are asked and which assumptions are used, so the honest response is to disclose the funder and test the findings against independent work. Excluding it outright is too blunt — funded research can still be methodologically sound, and the data it draws on may be accurate. Accepting it without qualification ignores the incentive to produce a favourable result, even when official statistics are used as inputs. The cue is to weigh a source, not simply accept or bin it.

questions.stem: Data shows Australia's real GDP grew by 1.5 per cent over a year while the population grew by 2.2 per cent. The most logical conclusion from this data is that:
options: output per person fell over the year, even though total output increased
the economy contracted over the year, since population growth exceeded output growth
living standards clearly improved, because total real output was higher than the year before
the economy was in recession, which is defined as GDP growth below population growth
questions.explanation: Real GDP rose, so total output grew, but because the population grew faster, the amount of output available per person went backwards — this is a fall in GDP per capita. Saying the economy contracted is wrong: real GDP growth of 1.5 per cent is positive growth, and population growth does not reduce the total. Claiming living standards clearly improved ignores that the same output is now shared among more people. Recession is conventionally described as consecutive quarters of falling real GDP, not growth below population growth.

questions.stem: In an economics investigation, which feature best indicates that a statistic has come from a verified source?
options: The publisher is identifiable and states how and when the data was collected
The figure appears at the top of the search results for the topic
The figure is repeated on several popular websites and social media pages
The wording around the figure is confident and free of qualifications
questions.explanation: Verification depends on being able to trace a statistic back to a named publisher and a stated method and collection date, so its accuracy and currency can be checked. The tempting option is that the figure is repeated on several popular websites and social media pages, but repetition only shows the number has been copied widely; unsourced figures spread just as easily as accurate ones. The cue is to ask 'who produced this, how, and when', not 'how often have I seen it'.

questions.stem: A report gives wage figures 'in real terms'. What does that mean?
options: They have been adjusted for inflation, so different years compare fairly
They have been raised by the inflation rate to estimate future worth
They are forecasts from a trend line rather than amounts actually recorded
They are the amounts actually paid before tax and superannuation
questions.explanation: Real values strip out the effect of changing prices, so a rise in real wages means purchasing power genuinely increased rather than just the dollar figure. The option about increasing figures by the inflation rate reverses the process: adjusting for inflation removes price effects from past data, it does not project values forward. The cue is that 'real' always contrasts with 'nominal' (the raw dollar figure) and always concerns comparison over time, not tax or forecasting.

questions.stem: The 'opportunity cost' of a chosen option is:
options: the extra paid when a dearer option is chosen over a cheaper one
the cost of the delay caused by researching the options first
the value of the next best alternative given up when choosing
the total money that must be spent to put the option into practice
questions.explanation: Because resources are scarce, choosing one response means forgoing others, and the opportunity cost is the benefit of the best alternative that was not taken. Naming the total amount of money spent is the common error — that is the monetary or financial cost, which appears directly on the cost side of the ledger. Opportunity cost is about the alternative sacrificed, not the dollars handed over.

questions.stem: A small business is considering a solar system costing $12,000 to install, which is expected to cut electricity bills by $2,400 a year for its 15-year life. Ignoring other factors, which conclusion does this cost-benefit analysis support?
options: The system pays for itself in about 5 years and delivers a net benefit of about $24,000 over its life
The system pays for itself in about 5 years and delivers a net benefit of about $36,000 over its life
The system takes about 12 years to pay for itself, so the benefits only just exceed the costs
The costs outweigh the benefits, because the $12,000 outlay is much larger than the $2,400 annual saving
questions.explanation: Total savings are 15 × $2,400 = $36,000, and subtracting the $12,000 cost leaves a net benefit of $24,000, with payback reached after $12,000 ÷ $2,400 = 5 years. Quoting $36,000 as the net benefit is the most tempting error, because that figure is the total benefit before the installation cost is deducted. Remember that 'net' always means benefits minus costs.

questions.stem: A takeaway shop is deciding whether to open for an extra evening shift. Estimates per week are: extra sales revenue $1,600; extra wages $900; extra stock $700; extra electricity $150. Ignoring other factors, what does this cost-benefit analysis support?
options: Not opening, because the extra weekly costs of $1,750 exceed the extra revenue of $1,600
Opening, because the extra revenue of $1,600 is larger than the $900 of extra wages the shift requires
Opening, because the $1,600 of extra revenue is money the business is currently not earning at all
Not opening, because the extra wages of $900 make up more than half of the extra revenue earned
questions.explanation: All the additional costs caused by the decision must be added together: 900 + 700 + 150 = $1,750, which is $150 more than the $1,600 of extra revenue, so the shift makes a weekly loss. Comparing revenue only with wages is the most tempting error, because it ignores stock and electricity, which are also caused by the decision. Revenue on its own is never a net benefit, and the share of revenue taken by wages is not the test. The cue: total every extra cost the option triggers before comparing.

questions.stem: A bakery is considering a $9,000 dough mixer. It would save 6 hours of paid labour a week at $30 an hour, but add $20 a week in maintenance. Ignoring other factors, which conclusion does this cost-benefit analysis support?
options: The saving of $180 a week repays the $9,000 in about 50 weeks, because maintenance is a running cost rather than part of the analysis
The purchase should be rejected, because the first year's saving of $8,320 is less than the $9,000 purchase price
The purchase gives no measurable benefit, because saved labour hours are not money coming into the business
The net saving of $160 a week repays the $9,000 in about 14 months, so the purchase is worthwhile if the mixer lasts well beyond that
questions.explanation: The weekly benefit is 6 × $30 = $180, minus the $20 maintenance cost, giving a net $160 a week, or $8,320 a year, so the $9,000 outlay is recovered in roughly 14 months and the mixer produces net gains for the rest of its life. Rejecting it because the first year's saving falls short of $9,000 is the tempting error: a cost-benefit analysis must cover the whole useful life of the asset, not an arbitrary 12 months. The cue is to match the time period of the benefits to the life of the investment.

questions.stem: A council is running a cost-benefit analysis on closing a shopping street to cars to create a pedestrian mall. Which listed item would be the hardest to convert into a reliable dollar figure?
options: The cost of the paving stones, seating and planter boxes bought for the mall
The parking meter revenue the council will no longer collect from that street
The extra travel time and inconvenience for residents who now have to park further away
The wages the council must pay the construction crew who build the new mall
questions.explanation: Cost-benefit analysis struggles with intangible costs — things people genuinely lose, such as time and convenience, that carry no market price and must be estimated indirectly. Lost parking meter revenue looks similar because it is a loss rather than a payment, but the council has past meter records and can put an exact dollar figure on it. The cue is whether a market price or existing record already exists for the item.

questions.stem: A company's cost-benefit analysis of a new quarry counts construction costs, wages and expected sales revenue, but does not include the dust and noise affecting nearby homes. The soundest evaluation of this analysis is that it:
options: is acceptable as presented, because dust and noise are environmental effects rather than economic costs
understates the net benefit, because effects on nearby residents belong on the benefits side of the ledger
is invalid, because a cost-benefit analysis can never take account of environmental or social effects
omits costs borne by third parties, so it overstates the net benefit of the quarry to the community
questions.explanation: Costs that fall on people outside the transaction are external costs, and leaving them out inflates the apparent net benefit of a project to society. Saying the analysis is acceptable because dust and noise are 'environmental' is the tempting error: anything that reduces people's wellbeing is an economic cost whether or not a bill is issued for it. A well-conducted cost-benefit analysis attempts to estimate such effects rather than ignoring them.

questions.stem: In evaluating a source, checking its 'validity' mainly means checking whether the:
options: document is genuinely from the author and organisation it claims to be from
information is written in formal language suitable for an academic report
source has been read and shared widely by other students and researchers
information actually measures what it claims to and supports the conclusions drawn
questions.explanation: Validity is about whether the data really measures what it says it measures and whether the reasoning from it holds up. Confirming the document is genuinely from the author and organisation named is authenticity, a related but different test — a genuine document can still contain invalid measures. Formal language and popularity say nothing about either quality. Cue: authenticity asks 'is it really from who it says?', validity asks 'does it really show what it says?'.

questions.stem: A 2011 report on internet shopping is used for a 2025 investigation. The main problem is its:
options: relevance, because household spending is unrelated to online retail
currency, because the data is too old to describe today's market
authenticity, because the report's author cannot be verified
sample size, because household surveys always survey too few
questions.explanation: Currency means how up to date a source is; online shopping has changed enormously since 2011, so the figures no longer describe the current market. Saying the authenticity is the problem is tempting, but nothing in the situation suggests the report is fake or misattributed — an old report can be perfectly genuine. Household spending data is clearly relevant to online retail, and sample size is not stated. Cue: ask 'is it real?' (authenticity) separately from 'is it still true?' (currency).

questions.stem: A survey asks: 'Do you agree that the government's unfair new levy should be scrapped?' Why does this weaken the validity of the results?
options: The wording leads respondents towards one answer, so responses may not reflect real views
The question is closed, and closed questions cannot produce valid data
The question is about government policy, and opinions on policy can never be measured
The question uses the word 'levy', so only economists could answer it accurately
questions.explanation: Calling the levy 'unfair' inside the question primes respondents to agree, so the data measures the wording's influence as much as genuine opinion — a validity problem. Blaming the closed format is tempting, but closed questions are widely used and produce perfectly valid data when worded neutrally. Opinions on policy are routinely and validly measured by surveys, and 'levy' is ordinary economic vocabulary. Cue: look for loaded adjectives before you judge the question format.

questions.stem: A blog post claims 'a leading study found small business closures doubled last year', but gives no author, date or link to the study. Before using this claim, the best action is to:
options: trace and read the original study to confirm the figure and its context
use the claim but describe it in the report as an estimate rather than a fact
search for other blogs repeating the same claim to confirm it is widely accepted
include the claim and note that the blog appeared high in the search results
questions.explanation: An unattributed claim cannot be evaluated at all until the original study is located, because only the original shows how 'closures' were defined and measured. Labelling it an estimate is tempting but does not fix anything — an unverified figure stays unverified no matter what you call it. Repetition across blogs shows circulation, not accuracy, and search ranking reflects algorithms rather than reliability. Cue: verification means going upstream to the source, not sideways to copies.

questions.stem: A student finds two sets of figures on youth wages: a peer-reviewed university study and a media release from a company promoting its own recruitment app. The soundest way to use them is to:
options: use only the media release, because it is the more recent and readable source
use both but weigh the study more heavily, noting the company's commercial interest
discard the media release entirely, because industry sources are always inaccurate
treat the two as equally reliable, since both are published and publicly available
questions.explanation: Evaluating sources means weighing them, not automatically accepting or rejecting: the peer-reviewed study has been checked by independent experts, while the media release has a clear commercial motive that may shape what it reports. Discarding the media release outright is tempting, but industry material can contain accurate, useful data and can be used with the interest declared. Public availability says nothing about rigour, and recency does not outweigh a conflict of interest. Cue: identify the source's purpose, then adjust how much weight you give it.

questions.stem: A student receives a screenshot of what appears to be an RBA statement announcing an interest rate change, shared through a group chat. Checking authenticity here means first establishing whether the:
options: image is clear enough to read and has no spelling errors in it
statement appears in that form on the Reserve Bank's own official website
figures in the statement match what economists had been forecasting
statement is consistent with what other students in the chat believe
questions.explanation: Authenticity is about whether a document genuinely originates from the body it claims, and a screenshot can be edited or fabricated, so the test is whether the same statement appears on the RBA's own site. Comparing the figures with forecasts is tempting, but forecasts are often wrong and a real announcement can surprise the market, so a mismatch proves nothing about origin. Group agreement and image quality are unrelated to whether the document is genuine. Cue: for authenticity, go to the issuing organisation's own publication.

questions.stem: Checking a source's authenticity mainly means establishing whether it:
options: presents figures in graphs and tables that are labelled and dated
reaches a conclusion matching the findings of other research
is genuinely what it claims, produced by the organisation named on it
measures the economic concept the investigation set out to measure
questions.explanation: Authenticity is about origin: is this document, dataset or statement really from the body it claims to come from, rather than altered, fabricated or misattributed. The option about measuring the concept the investigation set out to measure describes validity, which is a separate test applied after you know the source is genuine. A useful cue is that authenticity asks 'is it real and from whom it says?', while validity asks 'does it actually measure the right thing?'

questions.stem: A news website runs an online poll asking readers to click 'yes' or 'no' on whether the minimum wage should rise. It reports that 78 per cent of the 12,000 people who responded said yes. A student wants to use this as evidence of Australian public opinion. The strongest evaluation of this source is that it is:
options: low in validity, because a sample of 12,000 people is far too small to say anything about opinion
high in validity, because the large number of responses makes the percentage statistically representative
high in validity, because the question offered a simple yes or no and so contained no loaded wording
low in validity, because respondents chose themselves and are unlikely to represent the wider population
questions.explanation: A self-selected online poll only captures people who visit that site and choose to click, so the sample is biased towards that audience and towards people with strong views; size cannot fix that bias. The claim that 12,000 is too small is wrong, since properly drawn samples of one to two thousand can represent a national population well. The cue is to check how respondents were chosen, not how many there were.

questions.stem: In an economics report, a well-constructed argument is:
options: a claim stated firmly and repeated in the introduction, body and conclusion
a summary of every statistic found, in the order the sources were located
a list of the opinions held by affected groups, with no position taken
a claim supported by evidence and reasoning that links it to the claim
questions.explanation: An argument needs three parts: a position (the claim), evidence drawn from credible sources, and reasoning that explains why the evidence supports the position. Repeating a claim firmly in every section is tempting because strong arguments do state a clear position, but repetition adds no evidence and persuades nobody. The cue is that an argument must answer 'how do you know?' as well as 'what do you think?'

questions.stem: Used correctly, 'productivity' means:
options: the number of workers a business employs to produce its goods
the profit a business earns on each item it sells
the output produced per unit of input, such as output per hour
the total goods and services a country produces in a year
questions.explanation: Productivity is a ratio: output measured against the inputs used to make it, most often output per hour worked. 'The total quantity of goods and services produced in a year' is the most tempting distractor, but that is total output (GDP), which can rise simply because more people are working longer hours. The cue is the word 'per' — productivity is always output compared with input, not output on its own.

questions.stem: Why should an economics report reference its sources?
options: so the report reaches the word length without adding more analysis
because more references automatically means a better argument
because referencing removes the need to explain how evidence supports it
so the reader can check the evidence and judge how reliable it is
questions.explanation: Referencing makes an argument testable: the reader can trace each figure back to its origin and weigh up whether that origin is credible. 'More references means a better argument' is tempting because referencing is valued, but a long list of weak or irrelevant sources strengthens nothing. The cue is that references exist to serve the reader's checking, not to decorate the page.

questions.stem: In a report on housing affordability, which sentence is evidence rather than a claim?
options: Housing in Melbourne has become unaffordable for almost every young Australian worker
The government has failed to take housing affordability seriously over the past decade
Rising house prices are the single most serious economic problem facing Australia today
According to ABS data, the median Melbourne house price rose 8 per cent in the year to June
questions.explanation: Evidence is a verifiable statement attributed to a source; a claim is a position that must be argued for. The statement that housing is unaffordable for almost every young worker sounds factual, but 'almost every' is an unmeasured generalisation with no source attached, so it is a claim awaiting evidence. The cue is whether the sentence could be checked against published figures by someone else.

questions.stem: Australia 'entered a recession'. On the definition commonly used here, that means:
options: Two consecutive quarters of negative real GDP growth
Two consecutive quarters where inflation rose faster than wages
Two consecutive months in which unemployment increased
A fall of more than 10 per cent in average share prices
questions.explanation: The widely used working definition of a recession is two consecutive quarters (six months) of negative growth in real GDP, meaning the total value of goods and services produced actually shrank. The option about inflation outpacing wages is tempting because falling real wages feel like a downturn, but that describes a cost-of-living squeeze, not a recession. The cue is the measure: a recession is defined by output (real GDP), not by prices, jobs figures or share markets.

questions.stem: Which sentence best presents evidence with its source?
options: According to the ABS Labour Force release of June 2024, youth unemployment was 9.7 per cent.
Everyone knows youth unemployment is much higher than the national rate.
A website said youth unemployment was 9.7 per cent, so nobody can find work.
Youth unemployment was 9.7 per cent, which is deeply unfair.
questions.explanation: Referencing a source means naming who produced the data and when, so a reader can locate and check it, and then stating the figure accurately. The sentence beginning 'A website I looked at' is the closest rival because it does at least give a figure, but 'a website' identifies nothing checkable and 'proves' overstates what one statistic can show. The cue is whether a reader could find the original data from the words on the page.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'Last year the federal government cut the cash rate to encourage household spending.' What is the terminology error in this sentence?
options: Cutting the cash rate discourages household spending rather than encouraging it
The cash rate is set individually by each of the commercial banks
The rate the Reserve Bank sets is correctly called the exchange rate
The Reserve Bank of Australia, not the federal government, sets the cash rate
questions.explanation: Monetary policy in Australia is conducted independently by the Reserve Bank of Australia, which sets the cash rate target; the federal government controls fiscal policy such as taxes and spending. The option claiming a cash rate cut discourages spending is tempting if you reverse the mechanism, but lower rates reduce borrowing costs and typically support spending. The cue is to check who holds the policy lever before naming the actor in a sentence.

questions.stem: A Year 10 student is writing an argument on whether Australia should raise the minimum wage. Which approach produces the strongest economic argument?
options: State a clear position, support it with referenced data, then answer the main opposing view using evidence
State a clear position and restate it forcefully in every paragraph using strongly emotive language
Present all the data collected in the order it was found and let the reader decide the position
Present only the evidence that supports the position, leaving out figures that point the other way
questions.explanation: An argument is judged on whether its claims are supported by referenced evidence and whether it can withstand the strongest objection, so engaging with the counter-argument strengthens rather than weakens the case. Listing all data in the order it was found is tempting because it looks balanced and thorough, but a report that reaches no reasoned position is a data dump, not an argument. The cue is that strength comes from evidence and reasoning, not from repetition, emotion or leaving contrary evidence out.

questions.stem: What does 'opportunity cost' mean?
options: The price after a discount is applied
The value of the next best option given up
The total amount of money spent on a purchase
The cost of borrowing money for a year
questions.explanation: Every choice means giving something up, and the opportunity cost is the best alternative you did not take. It is not the price paid, which is why the money option is wrong even though it sounds like a cost.
questions.teaching:
Economics begins from scarcity: time, money and attention are all limited, so every choice rules something else out. This idea puts a price on whatever was ruled out.

That price is not the amount you paid. Spend Saturday at work earning $120 and the real cost of the decision is whatever you would otherwise have done with the day — the training session, a shift at a better-paying job, the sleep. Only the single most attractive alternative counts, not all of them added together, because you could only ever have taken one. It applies to things bought with no money at all: an hour of study carries a cost even though nothing changed hands. Governments reason the same way when a new hospital means a road that will not be built.

questions.stem: What is inflation?
options: A general rise in prices over time
A fall in the level of unemployment
An increase in the value of money
A rise in the number of businesses
questions.explanation: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level, which means each dollar buys less. Saying money increases in value gets it exactly backwards.
questions.teaching:
Individual prices move constantly for their own reasons. This term describes something broader: a sustained rise in the general price level across the economy.

In Australia it is measured through the Consumer Price Index, which tracks a fixed basket of household goods and services. The consequence is about money rather than goods: if everything costs more, each dollar buys less, so the purchasing power of money falls as the figure rises. The two move in opposite directions, which is the point most often reversed. The Reserve Bank targets 2–3% on average, since mild inflation is considered healthier than prices falling.

questions.stem: What does GDP measure?
options: The average income of each household in a year
The total money held in banks
The number of people in work
The total value of goods and services produced
questions.explanation: Gross domestic product totals what an economy produces in a period. It says nothing about how that output is shared, which is why GDP can rise while many households feel no better off.
questions.teaching:
This is the standard headline measure of the size of an economy, and knowing exactly what it counts also tells you what it misses.

It totals the market value of everything a country produces, both goods and services, over a period — usually a quarter or a year. Two consecutive quarters of it shrinking is the common working definition of a recession. What it does not capture matters just as much: it says nothing about how the output is shared, so it can rise while most households feel no better off. It also ignores unpaid work, volunteering and environmental damage, and counts rebuilding after a disaster as a gain.

questions.stem: What is a 'need' in economics?
options: Something that improves comfort
Something bought most often
Something that is expensive
Something essential for survival
questions.explanation: Needs are the essentials — food, water, shelter. Wants improve life without being essential, and the line between them is what most economic choices turn on.
questions.teaching:
Economics begins from scarcity, and the first distinction it draws is between two kinds of things people want.

One kind is required for survival — food, clean water, shelter, and in most modern definitions basic healthcare and clothing. The other kind improves life without being necessary for it. The line is not always obvious and shifts with time and society: a phone was clearly the second kind thirty years ago and is arguably closer to the first now if you need one to get work. The distinction matters because it underpins arguments about what governments should guarantee rather than leave to the market.

questions.stem: What does the Reserve Bank of Australia set?
options: The minimum wage
Company profits
The cash rate
Income tax rates
questions.explanation: The RBA sets the cash rate, which influences the interest rates banks charge. Tax rates are set by Parliament and the minimum wage by the Fair Work Commission, so each wrong option belongs to a different body.
questions.teaching:
Different bodies control different economic levers, and this question is about which lever belongs to which body.

The Reserve Bank is independent of government and sets the cash rate — the interest rate that flows through to what banks charge on mortgages and pay on savings. Raising it slows borrowing and spending to bring inflation down; lowering it does the opposite. Tax rates are set by Parliament through the budget, and the minimum wage is set annually by the Fair Work Commission. So each wrong option is a real decision made by a real body, just not this one.

questions.stem: What is a business's revenue?
options: The money it owes to its suppliers
The money invested by its owners
The total money it receives from sales
The money left after costs are paid
questions.explanation: Revenue is everything coming in from sales, before any costs. What is left after costs is profit, and treating the two as the same thing is the most common business-studies error.
questions.teaching:
A set of business accounts contains two figures that both sound like "how much it made", and treating them as the same thing is the most common error in this topic.

The first is everything coming in from customers over a period — the till total, before anything at all is deducted. Out of that the business still has to pay wages, rent, stock, electricity and interest. Whatever survives all of that is the second figure. A café can take $500,000 across a year and still shut, if its costs came to $520,000. That is why the first figure alone tells you almost nothing about whether a business is healthy, and why "we doubled our sales" is not the same claim as "we doubled our profit".

questions.stem: What does 'unemployment' mean?
options: Being retired from paid work
Being without work but looking for it
Being without work and not looking
Working fewer hours than you want
questions.explanation: To count as unemployed you must be without work and actively seeking it. Someone not looking is outside the labour force, which is why the unemployment rate can fall when people give up searching.
questions.teaching:
The official definition is narrower than everyday usage, and the narrowness is exactly what these questions test.

To be counted, a person must be without work, available to start, and actively looking for it. Someone who has given up searching is classified as outside the labour force rather than unemployed — which is why the headline rate can fall when discouraged workers stop looking, without any new jobs existing. Someone working one hour a week counts as employed. Underemployment, meaning working fewer hours than you want, is measured separately for exactly that reason.

questions.stem: What is superannuation?
options: Money saved during work for retirement
A tax paid on high incomes
A loan taken out to buy a house
Interest earned on a bank account
questions.explanation: Super is money set aside during working life to fund retirement, with employers required to contribute a set share of earnings. It is a savings arrangement, not a tax, though it is taxed differently.
questions.teaching:
This is Australia's system for funding retirement, and it is built on compulsory saving during working life rather than on a pension paid from tax alone.

Employers must contribute a set percentage of an employee's ordinary earnings into a fund, on top of wages — the Superannuation Guarantee, introduced in 1992. That money is invested and generally cannot be accessed until retirement age. It receives concessional tax treatment, which is why it grows faster than ordinary savings. Note it is a savings arrangement rather than a tax: the money remains the worker's, and the balance is theirs to draw on later.
